title: P0 Hosted API socket backlog ejection review
summary: Brief: A rapid influx of TLS renegotiations coincident with a gradual accept-queue shrinkage on our edge frontdoors caused accept() to fail briefly, triggering elevated 5xx rates and streaming fragmentation across multiple regions. The service had a ~20 minute high-error plateau followed by cascading retries that prolonged customer-visible latency. Root cause was a combination of kernel-level backlog sizing, an untested acceptor backpressure change pushed the week prior, and a thin thread pool handling TLS handshakes.
impact_summary:
- Duration: ~2h51m observable impact window; critical degradation for ~20 minutes at peak.
- Affected customers: ~14% of active hosted API tenants experienced elevated 5xx and streaming reconnects.
- Symptoms: p95 generation latency spiked from 180ms to 2.8s, 5xx rate rose from 0.02% baseline to 7.4% at peak, streaming session fragmentation and increased reconnects.
- Regions impacted: primary across us-west-2 and eu-west-1; spillover to other regions via global routing failover for a subset of customers.
timeline:
2029-11-20T03:12:00Z - First surge in SYN+TLS handshake retries detected on frontdoor metrics (small spike, ignored).
2029-11-20T03:28:00Z - p95 latency climbs above SLO on a handful of routes; 5xx begins to rise. Pager fired and SREs + frontdoor oncall joined.
2029-11-20T03:34:00Z - Streaming churn alerts show connection resets and partial payloads. Traces show accept() syscalls timing out / failing on several edge hosts.
2029-11-20T03:40:00Z - Short mitigation: scaled up frontdoor pool by adding 30% extra instances; errors dropped slightly but did not recover fully.
2029-11-20T03:50:00Z - Run rapid kernel inspection: netstat and /proc show many sockets in TIME_WAIT/CLOSE_WAIT and accept queue length at OS level near configured limit.
2029-11-20T03:58:00Z - Identified recently merged change (PR#8021) to acceptor backpressure behavior that reduces backlog reserve when CPU load is high. That change interacted poorly with a TLS-thread-pool exhaustion scenario.
2029-11-20T04:05:00Z - Emergency rollback of acceptor backpressure change deployed to edge fleet; immediate improvement in accept() success rate across hosts.
2029-11-20T04:18:00Z - Further mitigations: kernel bump of somaxconn and tcp_max_syn_backlog on affected hosts rolled via automation to raise accept queue ceilings for 12h as safety.
2029-11-20T04:45:00Z - 5xx and latency returned to near-baseline for majority customers; streaming reconnect rate stabilized.
2029-11-20T06:03:00Z - Incident declared resolved after monitoring window and verification with representative tenants.
root_cause: A three-way interaction: (1) a small recent code change to the acceptor backpressure heuristics (PR#8021) reduced the effective accept queue reserve under transient CPU pressure; (2) an up-tick in TLS renegotiations (caused by misbehaving SDK clients and a spike of clients switching networks) created bursts of handshake work that saturated the thin TLS-handshake thread pool; and (3) default kernel accept queue sizing (somaxconn / tcp_max_syn_backlog) on several edge hosts was at conservative values and permitted the accept queue to reach fullness quickly. Together this led to accept() failures and connection churn which cascaded into retries increasing load and prolonging the outage.
contributing_factors:
- PR#8021 was merged without a safety gate that limits the backlog reduction under TLS-heavy workloads.
- Lack of synthetic TLS-negotiation spike tests in our premerge suite.
- TLS thread pool size was tuned for steady-state memory footprint, not short-lived handshake spikes.
- Alerts were tuned to latency and 5xx thresholds but did not surface accept-queue saturation directly; visibility gap.
- Some customer SDKs aggressively retried on partial failures which amplified the load (retry amplification).
immediate_mitigation:
- Rolled back acceptor backpressure change (PR#8021) across edge fleet.
- Temporarily increased kernel backlog settings (somaxconn and tcp_max_syn_backlog) on affected hosts via automation playbook to reduce accept queue ejections.
- Scaled frontdoor instances to add capacity for TLS work.
- Opened a communication channel with top affected customers and applied per-tenant routing exemptions for streaming routes while cleanup completed.
long_term_actions: ENG-SERVING: Revert PR#8021 permanently or rework to include an explicit TLS-handshake safety gate (owner: Samir Joshi, due: 2029-12-10)
SRE: Add accept-queue length and accept-failure rate to SLO-adjacent alerts and dashboards (owner: Aisha Kumar, due: 2029-12-02)
INFRA: Update bootstrap AMI to set conservative somaxconn and tcp_max_syn_backlog defaults and expose runtime knobs via config (owner: Mateo Alvarez, due: 2029-12-08)
PLATFORM: Expand premerge test harness to include synthetic TLS-handshake burst tests and onboard representative SDK retry patterns (owner: Rina Patel, due: 2029-12-15)
PRODUCT: Work with Developer Experience to publish guidance for SDK retry backoff behavior and detect misbehaving SDK versions (owner: Ivy Chen, due: 2029-12-20)
SRE/ENG: Implement an adaptive TLS-handshake thread pool controller that temporarily increases pool size while preserving memory caps (owner: Samir Joshi, due: 2030-01-10)
OPS: Create an emergency runbook section 'accept-queue saturation' with automated diagnostics and a one-click rollback for acceptor heuristics (owner: Aisha Kumar, due: 2029-12-01)
post_incident_checks:
- Verify no remaining hosts are running the rolled-back acceptor code (automation verification done).
- Confirm backlog kernel tuning persisted across reboots for the AMI version used today.
- Run a scheduled synthetic TLS burst test against a staging replica to validate future behavior.
- Coordinate a customer outreach summary and append to incident timeline.
runbook_updates:
- New entry: 'accept-queue saturation' with the following diagnostics: check /proc/net/tcp backlog metrics, accept-failure counters, TLS-thread-pool utilization.
- Add automated rollback marker to any acceptor heuristic change: require a canary with synthetic handshake spike pass before full rollout.
- Add presubmit job that runs a short TLS-handshake-burst in CI for the frontdoor service.
lessons_learned:
- Small runtime heuristics can have outsized impact when orthogonal systems (kernel limits, TLS pools, client behavior) interact.
- Observable surface area must include OS-level accept/backlog metrics; high-level 5xx/latency alerts are necessary but not sufficient.
- Canary testing for network-facing heuristics must include synthetic protocol-level bursts, not just CPU/memory smoke tests.
- Customer SDK retry patterns can be the difference between a brief blip and an outage; invest in detection and guidance.
communication:
- Incident summary posted to #sre-incident with timeline and mitigations.
- Customer success sent targeted notifications to top 20 impacted tenants with technical details and remediation steps.
- Internal all-hands note and TL;DR for execs prepared by product and SRE.
